full.bigTake: The market enters Thanksgiving week after a rout. The S&P 500 fell 8.6% and the Nasdaq 100 10.5%; the S&P and Dow are in correction (more than 10% off their highs), every sector fell, and VIX closed at 35.89 with its near-term curve inverted. The story was the AI trade breaking under its own weight: Nvidia beat and raised Tuesday (revenue $115.8B vs $109.1B, Q4 guide ~$130B) but reversed Wednesday and fell 22.9% on the week after governance and legal headlines (a reported SEC civil probe of its disclosures, California's AG looking at chip diversion); Broadcom fell on a report that Google cut its Broadcom AI-chip plans, AMD on a short seller's China claims, software on Salesforce and Intuit, and the Anthropic IPO (priced $83, opened 110–115, closed Friday at 88.30) pulled money out of the rest of the group. I'm built by Anthropic, whose stock (ANT) listed last week; read ANT only as a supply and sentiment event. Policy added to it: a Commerce rule on overseas data centers serving China (Mon) and Trump's reported threat to bar U.S. firms from building AI data centers abroad (Fri). The data were mixed: retail sales firm, Philly Fed and continuing claims soft. The FOMC minutes said almost all officials see more hikes as likely and called AI demand a material inflation risk, so a December 9 hike stays priced even as the 10-year fell to 4.91%. This week is short and thin: PMIs Monday, Dell and Analog Devices Tuesday, and the Wednesday 8:30 stack (core PCE, GDP, claims, durable goods) plus the Beige Book, then a closed Thursday and a 1:00 p.m. Friday. Sunday-night futures opened higher after Bessent warned the Fed against aggressive tightening. The Movers Report has the multi-day thesis (the AI capex chain, the rotation and the scenarios); this brief has last week's numbers and this week's calendar.

The Democratic sweep on Tuesday was first read as gridlock: Wednesday the S&P rose 1.6% and Microsoft (+6.7%), Amazon (+6.2%) and Apple (+5.3%) had big days. This week brings the inflation test (CPI Tue, PPI Fri) and the funding test (CoreWeave and Nebius, then Applied Materials and Cisco). short.bigTake: Risk-off into a heavy week, but it is a tech sell-off, not a broad one. The Nasdaq lost 2% (−5.3% in October, its worst month since March 2025) as Alphabet (−12.6% Thursday) and Intel (≈−29% Friday) turned the AI-spending worry into a sell-off in chip suppliers, while health care, materials, utilities and small caps rose and the equal-weight S&P gained 0.8%. Hot data (GDP 3.4%, core PCE 3.1% y/y, confidence 91.7) keeps a December 9 hike the base case, yet the 10-year fell to 4.93% as money hid in bonds. This week the AI hardware chain reports into that fear: Apple and Palantir Monday, AMD, Super Micro, Arista Tuesday, Arm and Qualcomm Wednesday, with the midterms Tuesday and the October jobs report Friday. For what it all means over the next 1–2 weeks (capex chain, rotation, scenarios), read the Movers Report; this brief has the numbers and the calendar.

This week the AI hardware chain reports straight into that fear, the midterms land Tuesday, the Treasury sets its refunding Wednesday, and Friday's jobs report decides whether hike odds hold. full.bigTake: The market enters the heaviest week of earnings season in a risk-off tilt, but it is a rotation more than a rout. Mega-cap tech and the AI trade are being sold on spending worries (Meta's higher capex plan, Tesla's lower one), pushing the Nasdaq 100 to its second straight weekly loss and about 6% below its record. At the same time the equal-weight S&P, small caps, energy, health care and staples rose. Oil near $103 WTI and $117 Brent, with Iran headlines, keeps inflation expectations high (1-year expectations 4.7%) and keeps the Fed on a hiking path: a hold is priced for Wednesday, but a December hike is the base case. The week's outcome hinges on three things in about 36 hours: the Fed's tone Wednesday at 2:30, Microsoft and Alphabet that evening, and GDP/core PCE plus Amazon on Thursday. A hawkish Fed plus weak cloud numbers is the bad combination for tech; good cloud growth with spending discipline could spark a relief rally in the most-sold names.
